fields.position: Separates pretraining priors, visual capacity and pre-fusion placement; zero-initialized vision-only QKVO/SwiGLU puts capacity into early backbone layers while retaining joint attention.
fields.tradeoff: BLIP-2 places a Q-Former bottleneck between frozen vision and language models. Unbundling compares capacity placement and training under matched data/lifetime compute. Token compression and capacity placement are different interventions; local kernels cannot rank VQA or TTFT.

fields.title: Visual interface placement and dedicated capacity are different variables
fields.body: Unbundling inserts extra capacity into joint attention/FFNs; BLIP-2 extracts visual information with learned queries before a frozen LLM. Check the visual mask rather than modality isolation for the former, and frozen boundaries/query bottlenecks for the latter. Initial functional equality is not trained capability equality, and the existing small BLIP-2 negative result is not the new paper's large-model comparison.

fields.question: Why not rank Unbundling against BLIP-2 simply by visual token count?
fields.answer: BLIP-2 studies a query bottleneck between frozen models. Unbundling separates dedicated capacity, priors and placement while retaining joint attention. Token counts, trainable parameters and lifetime budgets differ and need matched experiments.
fields.example: Four queries can reduce tokens but lose details. Early vision-only FFNs add capacity without directly reducing tokens; these are not interchangeable benefits.

fields.summary: Added fixed-version methods and bounded components or explicit review-only coverage, separating author results, local diagnostics and high-cost non-reproduction.

fields.position: Fixes data/tokenization and compares architecture using FLOPs/token, tokens and a coupled LR/batch surface. Final decayed checkpoints and equally weighted eleven-domain validation are part of the protocol.
fields.tradeoff: Data Mixing Laws changes domain mixtures using pilot fits; ArchSpace controls architecture size and LR/batch. Coefficients are not interchangeable, and arithmetic replay is neither new fitting nor architecture search.

fields.title: Fix interventions and budget units before fitting loss
fields.body: A shared loss output does not imply the same research task. Data Mixing Laws takes a mixture simplex; ArchSpace fixes data and measures training FLOPs as C=MD. M is not parameter count, and conditional optimal LR scales with square-root batch. Old baseline coefficients cannot establish new-architecture gains without new pilots.

fields.question: Why does combining loss predictors not establish architecture evolution?
fields.answer: They model different interventions. Combining them requires real candidate training, checked extrapolation and unified budgets; registration or published coefficients do not execute and evaluate a new candidate.
fields.example: Changing mixture and architecture together requires controls to separate data and structural contributions.

fields.summary: Added fixed-version methods and bounded components or explicit review-only coverage, separating author results, local diagnostics and high-cost non-reproduction.

fields.position: Splits shared cores/private fibers, separately applies SIGReg, predicts stopped other-view representations and penalizes four private–shared correlations.
fields.tradeoff: CLIP maps paired images/text into one unit space with symmetric contrastive learning. D-JEPA studies information asymmetry and shared/private roles. Its exact alignment-only theorem is not an unconditional rejection of complete CLIP training.

fields.title: Shared alignment does not replace private-information preservation
fields.body: Alignment constrains retained information; it does not automatically preserve everything needed downstream. Visual details and question relations may need private fibers; omitting private–private decorrelation permits coordination. Local loss/gradient tests do not measure actual synergy, and existing Fashion-MNIST CLIP results are not matched-paper comparisons.

fields.question: Does D-JEPA establish that CLIP-style alignment is always wrong?
fields.answer: No. It concerns informational asymmetry and exactly aligned solutions, while CLIP also performs instance discrimination and retrieval. Match models, data and readouts before claiming task-information loss.
fields.example: Different questions about one scene are not equally informative views; image–caption retrieval has a different supervision structure.

fields.summary: Added fixed-version methods and bounded components or explicit review-only coverage, separating author results, local diagnostics and high-cost non-reproduction.

fields.position: Retains modality-specific LeJEPA spaces and uses a skipless translator for target-space InfoNCE. Centroids normalize each view before aggregation, and both target sides receive gradients.
fields.tradeoff: CLIP directly optimizes common-space image/text scores. DuoJEPA assigns matching pressure to residual-free translation while jointly training encoders. No direct own-space term means neither independent training nor guaranteed translatability.

fields.title: Shared-space matching and cross-space translation impose different geometry
fields.body: First identify the space of each score operand and which sides receive gradients. Duo compares translated sources with own targets, whereas CLIP compares own representations directly. Skipless removes identity shortcuts and needs dedicated initialization. The local single-head layer omits full LeJEPA and global negatives, so it does not reproduce unaligned medical-retrieval geometry.

fields.question: Why not replace DuoJEPA's bidirectional InfoNCE with CLIP loss?
fields.answer: CLIP compares own vectors. Each Duo term compares a translated source with an own centroid inside one target space. Replacing it changes geometry, centroid construction and encoder gradients.
fields.example: An own image vector is in image space; its translated version is in text space. The latter matches the own text vector.

fields.summary: Added fixed-version methods and bounded components or explicit review-only coverage, separating author results, local diagnostics and high-cost non-reproduction.

fields.position: Transfers a pretrained video DiT into pixel space through linear alignment, timestep calibration and a detailer, addressing high-resolution detail and temporal consistency. Review only locally.
fields.tradeoff: WOVEN turns action-conditioned rollouts into transition supervision for MLLM answers. PixVid changes the generator's representation/compute path. Sharper generation does not establish action/causal correctness or multiple-choice accuracy.

fields.title: Generating video and learning transitions require separate acceptance
fields.body: A video generator can supply transition-training data, but visual quality, action fidelity, state consistency and downstream reasoning need separate checks. The full 14B/1.3-million-clip PixVid matrix is not run. Existing small WOVEN SFT negative results do not predict PixVid benefits. No local joint system is claimed.

fields.question: Would replacing WOVEN's generator with PixVid establish stronger transition reasoning?
fields.answer: No. First evaluate action/state fidelity, then train/evaluate downstream models under fixed data protocols. Image clarity covers only one axis; no such combination was run here.
fields.example: A sharper but incorrect action outcome still supplies incorrect downstream transition supervision.

fields.summary: Added fixed-version methods and bounded components or explicit review-only coverage, separating author results, local diagnostics and high-cost non-reproduction.

fields.position: Connects CLIP and other SSL through spectral representations, distinguishes unbiased objectives, fixed-negative surrogates and biased plug-ins, and derives U-statistic penalties excluding same-sample terms. Fixed-v4 theory intake only.
fields.tradeoff: CLIP provides executable image/text contrastive models; Spectral Ghost analyzes parametrizations and estimators. Unbiasedness/consistency does not rank task accuracy. Historical Google bylines do not replace v4 affiliations.

fields.title: Estimator bias and multimodal alignment geometry are different axes
fields.body: InfoNCE negative counts affect more than variance: under misspecification they can change surrogate optima. Non-contrastive squared-covariance plug-ins can be biased through same-sample terms. Audit geometry, objectives, independent sampling and optimization budgets separately rather than infer cost/capability from labels. There is no source empirical matrix and no invented expensive deferred experiment.

fields.question: Does unbiasedness analysis prove smaller CLIP batches are better?
fields.answer: No. Unbiasedness differs from variance, statistical efficiency and misspecification; a fixed-negative ranking-NCE surrogate has its own optimum. Objective theory is not a downstream performance ranking.
fields.example: Removing same-sample bias can still leave large finite-batch variance. Accuracy and convergence need experiments that this paper does not supply.

fields.summary: Added fixed-v4 theoretical methods and versioned affiliation evidence without inventing training experiments or local metrics.

fields.position: Reuse verified lemmas in a persistent AND–OR DAG, alternating informal blueprints, Lean sketches, compiler feedback and semantic decomposition review; preserve v1 publication while reviewing v3.
fields.tradeoff: DRAGO tests specification fidelity/non-regression; LEAP must also reject formally valid but unproductive decomposition. Formal validity, useful search and task fidelity are distinct, with no reference leakage.

fields.title: Formal verification checks the expressed claim, not whether it is useful or intended
fields.body: A solvable DRAGO specification may omit the original goal, motivating diagnostics and anti-degradation. A type-correct LEAP sketch may rename its parent as a child lemma, requiring semantic review for progress. Deterministic checks and external semantics remain separate; STRIPS kernels or generic DAGs do not replace Lean proving or language fidelity.

fields.question: Do a Lean-accepted sketch and a DRAGO planner's valid plan each establish completion?
fields.answer: No. A sketch may retain unproved/unhelpful lemmas; a plan may solve a weakened or incorrect specification. Necessary obligations, useful progress and task fidelity require separate checks.
fields.example: Teaching example: assuming the target theorem trivially entails it but does not prove it.

fields.summary: Add Google LEAP's historical v3 revision, separating formal validity, useful decomposition and task fidelity while retaining June publication and November revision.

fields.position: Value memory through matched-state future-task rollouts and gate its overall value to traceable first-use steps.
fields.tradeoff: MemPrice allocates context capacity/fidelity; CoReMem optimizes future resolution/work. Token occupancy, action steps and semantic utility differ, and local kernels generate no memory.

fields.title: Memory price, value and credit require distinct measurement contracts
fields.body: MemPrice trades externally estimated utility against token size under a hard budget, adapting long-run retention through a pressure queue. CoReMem requires future tasks from an identical inherited repository, a success-first reward and anchor-based traceability. Neither local kernel fills in external semantic models: fewer tokens do not imply fewer actions, and an anchor is not causality.

fields.question: Must lower memory-token occupancy increase CoReMem prospective value?
fields.answer: No. Compression may remove a needed future check. CoReMem measures later resolution/work from identical inherited states; MemPrice capacity and this reward are not interchangeable.
fields.example: Teaching example: removing a short test command saves a few tokens but may add ten exploration steps.

fields.summary: Value memory through matched-state future-task rollouts and gate its overall value to traceable first-use steps. MemPrice allocates context capacity/fidelity; CoReMem optimizes future resolution/work. Token occupancy, action steps and semantic utility differ, and local kernels generate no memory.

fields.position: Trusted schemas derive authority, exact request grounding limits values, pre-read commitment limits actions, and the first failure stops remaining effects.
fields.tradeoff: RuntimeTickets narrows host grants through sourced obligations and cumulative budgets. CapLite trusts schemas/request. Both need all effects mediated; callbacks are not network isolation.

fields.title: Pre-effect checks must expose the origin of their authority
fields.body: CapLite removes model-written security policy in favor of trusted schemas, request grounding and write commitments. RuntimeTickets allows proposed obligations but freezes source-backed host-approved tickets before checking objects and budgets. Neither permits untrusted observations to authorize effects or protects tools that bypass mediation. Security is more than an allow flag.

fields.question: Can grounded CapLite arguments replace RuntimeTickets cumulative limits?
fields.answer: No. Grounding says values occur in the request, not how many times or bytes legal actions may accumulate. Separate grant/budget and replay contracts are required.
fields.example: Teaching example: one authorized email does not authorize a thousand repeated deliveries.

fields.summary: Trusted schemas derive authority, exact request grounding limits values, pre-read commitment limits actions, and the first failure stops remaining effects. RuntimeTickets narrows host grants through sourced obligations and cumulative budgets. CapLite trusts schemas/request. Both need all effects mediated; callbacks are not network isolation.

fields.position: Build task/seed/reflection role groups, value handoffs through fresh downstream actors, and update one shared model using a joint generated-token mean.
fields.tradeoff: GiGPO separates trajectory macro and shared-anchor-state micro credit. ACE-RL groups handoff provenance, not convergent states. Without real actors/environments only formulas/control contracts are measured.

fields.title: Group-relative credit begins with what each group compares
fields.body: GiGPO separates whole-trajectory reward from action differences at a shared anchor state. ACE-RL groups actor tasks, reflector seeds and curator reflections, valuing edits through new execution rather than prose scoring. Shared centering does not equal shared provenance, counterfactuals or information boundaries. Singleton filters/token reductions also change training and cannot be hidden in one generic normalizer.

fields.question: Does one task-level GRPO group combining actors, reflectors and curators preserve ACE-RL?
fields.answer: No. Their rewards and comparison provenance differ. Preserve seed/reflection groups before concatenating generated tokens for a shared update.
fields.example: Teaching example: three edits from one reflection compare with each other, not directly with a separate actor's task score.

fields.summary: Build task/seed/reflection role groups, value handoffs through fresh downstream actors, and update one shared model using a joint generated-token mean. GiGPO separates trajectory macro and shared-anchor-state micro credit. ACE-RL groups handoff provenance, not convergent states. Without real actors/environments only formulas/control contracts are measured.

fields.position: Apply existing harness optimization to real multi-agent search, retain history and analyze persistent orchestration failures; no new optimizer is proposed.
fields.tradeoff: HarnessLens emphasizes paired behavior-relevant attribution gates. MULTILOOP gains mostly concern prompts/tools; higher aggregate accuracy does not establish coordination repair, nor do ten tasks imply cheap APIs.

fields.title: Optimization gains do not establish causal orchestration improvement
fields.body: MULTILOOP lets a coding optimizer edit harnesses from traces but finds persistent orchestration failures. HarnessLens narrows acceptance to affected behavior tasks with paired attribution evidence. Search, acceptance and mechanism explanation differ; without real models/tools a loop measures control flow, not the published gains.

fields.question: Does increased MULTILOOP accuracy show subagent delegation is repaired?
fields.answer: No. Prompt-only/tool changes can explain much of the gain while orchestration faults remain. Attributing gains to delegation requires relevant controlled evidence.
fields.example: Teaching example: adding PDF retrieval can improve scores without fixing duplicate task assignment.

fields.summary: Apply existing harness optimization to real multi-agent search, retain history and analyze persistent orchestration failures; no new optimizer is proposed. HarnessLens emphasizes paired behavior-relevant attribution gates. MULTILOOP gains mostly concern prompts/tools; higher aggregate accuracy does not establish coordination repair, nor do ten tasks imply cheap APIs.

fields.position: Gate strategy readiness before dependency-aware proof work, preserve critiques in overlapping-tree synthesis, and route global findings to repair/re-exploration while isolating grading from selection.
fields.tradeoff: ScientistTwo controls subset/full experiments and review loops; Colosseum reviews mathematical assumptions/dependencies. Shared stage structure does not make semantic judges or sufficient evidence interchangeable.

fields.title: Research controllers succeed through domain evidence, not a generic success label
fields.body: ScientistTwo promotes executable experiments and performs ablation/strict comparison; Colosseum uses readiness and local/global falsification for long proofs. Failure to find a counterexample is not correctness, just as simulated review is not conference acceptance. Full systems need costly external research semantics; generic trees/callbacks do not inherit these capabilities.

fields.question: Can reference-proof candidate selection count as a stronger ScientistTwo-style review?
fields.answer: No. References belong only to the final benchmark grader. Providing them to selection misrepresents an oracle best-of-two ceiling as reasoning ability; research review also needs held-out boundaries.
fields.example: Teaching example: reading the standard solution before picking a paper is not leakage-free autonomous research.

fields.summary: Gate strategy readiness before dependency-aware proof work, preserve critiques in overlapping-tree synthesis, and route global findings to repair/re-exploration while isolating grading from selection. ScientistTwo controls subset/full experiments and review loops; Colosseum reviews mathematical assumptions/dependencies. Shared stage structure does not make semantic judges or sufficient evidence interchangeable.

fields.position: Gate whole responses by detached current-policy mean log probability; sum retained token advantages and average over all responses without old-policy ratios.
fields.tradeoff: Dr. GRPO removes group/length normalization; LGPO selects response gradients. These are different axes. Negative high-likelihood advantages are gated too, and tiny-logit checks prove neither LLM stability nor speed.

fields.title: Gradient membership and advantage scale are independent design axes
fields.body: Dr. GRPO keeps centered rewards while removing group-std and length biases. LGPO supplies no new reward estimator; it removes whole-response gradients above a current-policy mean-logp threshold. Renormalizing survivors changes step scale by acceptance rate, not by the same operation as removing std. Comparisons or combinations must fix sampling policies, advantage scales, valid tokens and the all-response denominator. The authors' two-H100 timing is not local acceleration evidence.

fields.question: Should LGPO divide by survivors to compensate when half the responses are gated?
fields.answer: Not under this fidelity contract. The expectation averages all responses and assigns zero to gated ones. Survivor division increases the effective step size. Dr. GRPO's removed std does not establish equivalence for this denominator change.
fields.example: Teaching example: four responses, two retained and total contribution six give -6/4, not -6/2.

fields.summary: Add current-likelihood LGPO gating separately from Dr. GRPO advantage scaling. Preserve both advantage signs, token sums and the all-response denominator. Full LLM training is not reproduced due to cost; local gradients are not capability or speed evidence.

fields.position: Keep raw base rewards, use training-trajectory PAV maps only in penalties/dual control, and retain multiplier scaling with advantages that do not divide by total-reward std.
fields.tradeoff: Dr. GRPO removes std to address optimization biases; here that arithmetic also determines whether constraints affect learning. Ranking and mean level differ. A monotone CPU map proves neither VLM safety nor budget satisfaction.

fields.title: Preserving multiplier scale and calibrating cost are separate requirements
fields.body: Dr. GRPO-style unscaled advantages prevent total-reward group std from canceling multipliers, but biased scorer means can still saturate or deactivate the dual. Safety as a Budget maps only penalties/control using training trajectories while raw base rewards preserve within-group differences. PAV plateaus, data separation, EMA state and interpolation need explicit contracts. Monotonicity is not calibration, and per-objective standardized results are not local unscaled outcomes.

fields.question: Does removing std in a Dr. GRPO-style update make the safety budget a true event rate?
fields.answer: No. It preserves gradient scaling by the multiplier, but the budget still reads scorer means. Uncorrected bias can stabilize the controller at the wrong level. Independent labels, training-only fitting, held-out evaluation and explicit state remain necessary.
fields.example: Teaching example: gradient scaling is preserved, but a scorer that always understates harmfulness can still drive lambda to zero.

fields.summary: Add Safety as a Budget to separate advantage scaling from control-level calibration. Only training-limited PAV, two-channel rewards and explicit EMA dual arithmetic are local, not safety training; the high-cost full matrix is not reproduced.

fields.position: Use private-probe versus policy external-reward mean gaps to decide whole-group inversion, then remove probes; Eqs.3–5 only.
fields.tradeoff: TAG selects an anchor by reverse KL from separately trained probe policies, then gates auxiliary reward. Bait probes environment preferences, a different object. Numeric gaps do not prove probe semantics or safety; conflicting std conventions are not guessed.

fields.title: Specify probe provenance before deciding which reward object to transform
fields.body: TAG trains one policy per reward from a common baseline and selects an anchor with reverse KL on probe-generated samples. Bait privately marks special responses, compares environment reward preferences and flips the whole group. Both need actual probe provenance, not evaluator gold manufacturing perfect signals. Local Bait generates no text or attack: it checks the >=0 boundary and policy-only output. TAG's zero-anchor gating does not replace this sign rule.

fields.question: Can a trusted TAG anchor directly serve as Bait's private probe mask?
fields.answer: No. TAG selects a reward dimension through trained probe policies; Bait membership identifies response provenance within a group. Inputs, sampling and trust assumptions differ and need separate verification. Neither numeric core establishes the other's real safety.
fields.example: Teaching example: in a group of three responses, a TAG correctness-anchor score does not identify which response came from a defender probe.

fields.summary: Add Google DeepMind-related Bait reward-gap/sign-flip defense alongside TAG anchor gating, distinguishing probe provenance and transformed objects. Only Eqs.3–5 are implemented, with no harmful probes, attacks or training. The source std discrepancy is retained; full experiments are not reproduced due to cost.

fields.position: Independent-subspace parallel SIDs, training-prior calibration and prefix semantic-potential guidance, followed by Hamming/beam-score candidate recovery.
fields.tradeoff: TIGER quantizes successive residuals; ReSID changes both token structure and candidate reachability, not merely tail bonuses. Local frozen-input kernels train neither quantizers nor generators.

fields.title: Representing an item with a semantic ID does not make it survive a narrow beam
fields.body: TIGER encodes content with residual SIDs. ReSID highlights how quantization and early pruning can make tail items unreachable. Independent subspaces isolate errors, log-prior and log-mean-exp potentials guide prefixes, and partial matching tolerates local code errors. These operate at different stages. Gold similarities must not manufacture improvements, and exact finite-score checks establish neither 10.3ms serving nor revenue.

fields.question: Can a final ReSID reranker recover a low-probability exact TIGER SID?
fields.answer: Only if candidates or sufficiently close SIDs already survived. Early-pruned branches require decoding-stage treatment. ReSID also changes independent quantization and partial matching, so it is not just final-list scoring.
fields.example: Teaching example: keeping only prefix zero when the target lies below one leaves no target for the final reranker.

fields.summary: Add ReSID with quantified production A/B, separating parallel/residual IDs, prefix reachability and final ranking. CPU kernels are not recommender training or production evidence; full industrial experiments are not reproduced due to cost.

fields.position: Fixed-window trigger-tail injection, pristine-history trigger/default paths, a pooled router and independent level PFFNs condition generation.
fields.tradeoff: TIGER defines content quantization and autoregressive ID retrieval; TriGen addresses immediate-trigger versus historical-preference conflict. Local differentiable conditions omit full encoders/decoders, and random gradients are not recall.

fields.title: Which history supplies a condition matters more than adding another vector
fields.body: TIGER generates SIDs from history; TriGen also models recent-click redirection. Tail-injected encoder input may couple trigger/history, but dual paths read pristine history to preserve default preferences. The router pools paths before per-level weights; independent PFFNs do not authorize future SIDs. Record generation training, masks and GPU kernels separately; six-market author lifts do not validate random local layers.

fields.question: May both TriGen paths read the trigger-appended TIGER history?
fields.answer: Not under fixed v1. Injected history supplies the encoder, while both condition paths separately read pristine history so default queries remain trigger-independent. Dropping pristine history defeats the separation.
fields.example: Teaching example: changing only the trigger must leave the default path identical rather than steering it through repeated triggers.

fields.summary: Add TriGen with six-market production A/B, preserving fixed-window injection, pristine dual paths, position-specific PFFNs and observed-prefix boundaries. Local forward/backward is not full recommendation training; the high-cost industrial matrix is not reproduced.

fields.position: Daily user-wise validation, instance-weighted FullMonth and one-retrieval behavior evaluation define the continual protocol; local code supplies finite split/HR/NDCG interfaces.
fields.tradeoff: TIGER is a model; KuaiRecV2 benchmarks different models under dynamic item pools. The official link returned API404. L0 interfaces imply neither official-data ingestion nor capability rankings.

fields.title: A model name does not align evaluation time, and monthly means must not hide daily drops
fields.body: Static TIGER retrieval and KuaiRecV2 dynamic pools answer different questions. Daily validation retains each user's last daily event; FullMonth weights instances while trajectories reveal adaptation/forgetting. Behavior subsets reuse one request list and evaluator gold cannot flow to producers. The local L0 interface has no pool builder, history, official data or model, so finite HR cannot rank against actual local TIGER NDCG.

fields.question: Can HR=1 on a finite KuaiRecV2 example be compared with TIGER MovieLens NDCG?
fields.answer: No. The former is a model-free, unofficial-data L0 protocol example; the latter comes from specific data and real training. Tasks, pools, time axes and evidence tiers differ. Capability comparison requires actual models/official data under the same protocol and budget.
fields.example: Teaching example: correct discounts on two handwritten requests are not retrieval across thirty days and roughly 484 million interactions.

fields.summary: Add the KuaiRecV2 public protocol entry, clarifying daily validation, instance weighting and single-retrieval evaluate-all. Official repository accessibility is unverified, not a completed benchmark integration; full large-scale evaluation is not reproduced due to cost.
